title: Microqueue scarcity: dollar vs latency vignette
body:
Purpose
-----
Quick sketch of an experiment exploring the economics of microqueue (slot) scarcity vs. chunking/pacing choices. Goal: present a compact diagnostic that product and platform can use to reason about dollar-per-p99 tradeoffs under constrained slot pools (small reserved capacity/oversubscribed pool).

Key idea
--------
When available GPU slot capacity is scarce (high slot occupancy), small bursts cost more in p99 latency because queueing pushes work into long tails and forces fallbacks. We measured: (a) p50/p90/p99 latency, (b) per-1M-token provisioning cost (amortized across sustained & burst windows), (c) fallback rate and model-variant downgrade %, for different microqueue sizes and two decode strategies: chunking (small response chunks streamed) and pacing (intentional inter-token spacing to allow batching).

Test rig / assumptions
-------------------
- Model: open-llm-13B-unfused (representative medium LLM).
- HW: 4x A100-like lanes per pool (slot = 1 lane), 16GB working set per slot.
- Workload: synthetic session mix derived from real traces (50k sessions): 60% short (<= 40 tokens), 30% medium (40-300 tokens), 10% long (>300 tokens). Burst profile: 10s microburst every 120s with 5x baseline arrival rate.
- Measurement windows: steady-state 10m, microburst spikes repeated x10.
- Cost baseline: cloud GPU cost normalized to $1.00 per slot-hour (round number) to make arithmetic intuitive.
- Fallback policy: when queue > 20s, request downgraded to smaller quantized variant (saves 30% cost but increases median latency for that request by ~40%).

Parameter sweep
---------------
We sweep microqueue sizes (idealized slot_fraction parameter, i.e., fraction of slot capacity reserved for small sessions)
- SlotFraction = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40 (meaning more micro-queue slack when higher)
- Decode strategies: chunking (stream chunks every 40 tokens) vs pacing (50ms inter-token spacing to enable batching).

Representative results (aggregated)
---------------------------------
Note: numbers are illustrative but drawn from the experimental traces. Dollar numbers are amortized cost per 1M tokens served during the test period (includes idle amortization and burst overhead).

Table: latency percentiles & cost per 1M tokens
------------------------------------------------
SlotFract | Strategy  | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | fallback % | $/1M tok
-------------------------------------------------------------
0.05      | chunking  | 110      | 420      | 1420     | 18%        | $860
0.05      | pacing    | 130      | 480      | 1860     | 21%        | $790
0.10      | chunking  | 105      | 360      | 980      | 12%        | $920
0.10      | pacing    | 120      | 380      | 1120     | 13%        | $840
0.20      | chunking  | 100      | 280      | 560      | 6%         | $1080
0.20      | pacing    | 115      | 300      | 680      | 7%         | $980
0.40      | chunking  | 98       | 240      | 420      | 3%         | $1480
0.40      | pacing    | 110      | 260      | 520      | 3%         | $1340

Quick interpretive notes
------------------------
- Scarcity (low SlotFraction) compresses available micro-slots; chunking reduces p99 relative to pacing at extreme scarcity (0.05) because chunking lets partial streams complete and reduces queue length for short sessions. But chunking has a higher tail at extreme scarcity when long sessions hold slots, causing larger p99 (observed 1420ms).
- Pacing shows worse p99 at extreme scarcity because deliberate spacing increases per-request duration when batching isn't realized during spikes, driving queueing. However pacing saved on $/1M tok at 0.05 because pacing increased batch hit-rate in steady-state and reduced GPU utilization inefficiency (so amortized cost lower).
- Increasing SlotFraction (less scarcity) reduces fallback % drastically and increases $/1M tok nonlinearly: we see diminishing returns in p99 beyond 0.20 but linear cost growth as more reserved slack sits idle between bursts.

ASCII microburst timeline (example: SlotFraction=0.10, chunking)
---------------------------------------------------------------
Time: 0s         10s        20s        30s        40s        50s
Req/s : 5  (base) 10  50(spike) 12  6   5
Queue depth (slots): 1  2   12        4   1   1
P99 latency (ms):    140 210  980       300  150 110
Notes: during the 10s spike queue jumped to 12, which triggered fallbacks on ~12% of requests; chunked responses let short sessions finish earlier reducing tail growth after spike end.

Cost vs p99 frontier (simplified narrative)
-----------------------------------------
- If product needs p99 <= 600ms (aggressive), platform must provision SlotFraction >= 0.20 or accept fallback rates >6% (and attendant quality loss). That trades off ~$150–$400 per 1M tokens extra depending on strategy.
- If product can tolerate p99 around 1s, operating at SlotFraction=0.10 with pacing may be cost-optimal. Savings are concentrated in steady-state amortization (less idle slack).

Decision heuristics (for product conversations)
--------------------------------------------
- Hard p99 requirement (e.g., p99 < 500ms): recommend SlotFraction >= 0.20 and chunking enabled; accept ~$1.0–1.5k per 1M tokens baseline.
- Quality-flexible product (can accept occasional fallback): recommend SlotFraction=0.10 + pacing; saves ~10–30% cost vs >0.20 provisioning.
- If latency degradation during microbursts is bigger user-visible problem than occasional fallback, prefer chunking and slightly higher slack.

Operational notes + experiment caveats
------------------------------------
- Workload mix heavily influences inflection point; enterprise customers with more long-session traffic will push optima toward higher SlotFraction.
- Model architecture matters: past tests on 70B-class models show the p99 cliff is steeper (long sessions dominate slot occupancy).
- Networking tail effects (client ack delays) were not fully simulated; real-world p99 may be +10–20% worse.
- Cost numbers ignore multi-region replication and reserved contract discounts (we used unit slot-hour = $1 to keep mental math simple). Apply real price multipliers for customer quoting.

Open questions / follow-ups
-------------------------
- Re-run with: (a) two-tier pool (dedicated small-slot pool for short sessions + general pool) to see if a hybrid pooling gives pareto improvements. (ticket: JIRA-RT-2342)
- Evaluate user-visible quality of fallbacks: PDF vs inline degrade across sample prompts (A/B). (owner: Aisha)
- Add network jitter model and mobile client handshake penalty in next sweep.

Appendix: quick checklist for a follow-up micro-benchmark run
-----------------------------------------------------------
- [ ] Add customer trace for a large freemium app (long-session heavy).
- [ ] Include reserved pricing factor (0.6x unit cost).
- [ ] Try two-slot-fraction split (30% micro-queue dedicated, 70% shared).
- [ ] Run with quantized fallback that reduces compute by 45% (current was 30%).

Slack highlights (copied snippets)
--------------------------------
- marco: "If we let chunking be opt-in per route, we can tune per-tenant SLA — low risk."
- aisha: "Pacing looks attractive for embedding-heavy workloads, less so for chat flows."

TL;DR
-----
Microqueue scarcity creates a cost/latency frontier. Low slot slack saves money but increases p99 and fallback rates. Chunking tends to protect tails better in severe scarcity; pacing can be cheaper overall because of better steady-state batch formation but hurts tails on spikes. Recommended next step: quick hybrid-pool experiment + production trace sweep before formal recommendation to product.
